text: José María Hipólito Figueres Ferrer (25 September 1906 – 8 June 1990) was a Costa Rican politician who served three terms as President: 1948–1949, 1953–1958, and 1970–1974. Born on 25 September 1906 in San Ramón, Alajuela province, he was the eldest of four children of Mariano Figueres Forges, a doctor, and Francisca Ferrer Minguella, a teacher from Catalonia, and his first language was Catalan. In 1924, he traveled to Boston, United States, to study hydroelectric engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, returning to Costa Rica in 1928 where he purchased a farm in the mountains of San Cristóbal, Desamparados, naming it "La Lucha Sin Fin," which remained his home and operational base until his death. He became a successful coffee grower and rope manufacturer, employing over 1,000 sharecroppers and factory laborers, describing himself as a "farmer-socialist" and providing housing, medical care, recreation, a community vegetable farm, and free milk for workers' children. Sharecroppers could sell hemp grown on his plantation to him at market price or elsewhere if offered a better price. After returning to Costa Rica in 1944 following two years in exile for criticizing President Rafael Ángel Calderón Guardia, he founded the Democratic Party, which became the Social Democratic Party, intended as a counterweight to the ruling National Republican Party (PRN). The Calderón government, accused of corruption and implementing social reforms, inspired opposition. Figueres trained the Caribbean Legion, an irregular force of 700, which planned to overthrow the Costa Rican government and remove Central American dictators; U.S. officials closely monitored the group, especially after a series of terrorist attacks in 1945–1946 failed to spark a general strike. The 1948 presidential election, which allegedly saw Otilio Ulate defeat Calderón, was invalidated by Calderón supporters, leading to armed conflict and a 44-day civil war with over 2,000 deaths—Costa Rica’s bloodiest 20th-century event. Figueres led a provisional junta, the Founding Council, for 18 months, during which he enacted 834 reforms, calling it a deeper and more human revolution than Cuba’s. His social reforms mirrored Calderón’s 1943 Labor Code, with the difference being that Figueres had the power to implement them, supported by broad national consensus. He admired Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, noting the U.S. had allowed dictators to rise in exchange for anti-communism. In 1953, he founded the Partido Liberación Nacional (PLN), the most successful political party in Costa Rican history, and returned to power. He nationalized the banking sector, promoted private and national industry, and strengthened the middle class. U.S. officials were alarmed by his support for the Caribbean Legion, though he later criticized U.S. backing of dictators, boycotting the 1954 inter-American meeting held in Caracas, where Marcos Pérez Jiménez ruled. He cooperated with North American military plans, with more Costa Rican police graduating from the School of the Americas than any other nation except Nicaragua between 1950 and 1965. In 1957, he was the target of an assassination attempt by Cuban exiles, including Herminio Díaz García, acting under orders from Nicaraguan dictator Luis Somoza Debayle and Dominican dictator Rafael Trujillo; they were arrested, confessed to receiving $200,000 and aid from Trujillo to overthrow Batista, and received a six-month sentence. His support for the Caribbean Legion led to accusations during his second term; after an invasion of Nicaragua in April 1954 by anti-Somoza exiles linked to the Legion, Somoza launched a counter-attack, allowing former Costa Rican president Rafael Calderón to invade in January 1955. Somoza withdrew but secured a commitment from Figueres to sever ties with the exiles. In 1958, during a visit to Caracas, U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon was attacked by anti-American protesters who damaged his motorcade and injured Venezuela’s foreign minister; the U.S. Congress formed a special committee to investigate, with Figueres testifying on 9 June 1958, condemning the Venezuelans and criticizing U.S. support for Trujillo, resource extraction, and autocracy. Economic threats from the termination of Alliance for Progress funds and the collapse of the Central American Common Market were mitigated when Figueres sold 30,000 tons of coffee to the Soviet Union in 1972, making Costa Rica the only Central American nation to establish diplomatic relations with Moscow; the World Bank and IMF provided millions to stabilize the economy. In 1971, when Nicaraguan rebels seized a plane flying from Managua to Miami and held passengers hostage, demanding fuel for a flight to Cuba, Figueres ordered Costa Rican police to disable the plane’s engines and tires; the hijackers demanded a new plane, which was agreed to, and hostages were released; when the hijackers exited, Figueres, 160 centimeters tall with a submachine gun, met them with 200 armed police, resulting in a shootout that killed two. He nearly derailed a 1973 Central American summit by criticizing five army generals, saying, "Isn't it odd that all you bastards are generals, and I'm the only civilian, but I'm the only one who's ever fought a war?" According to the Mitrokhin Archive, the KGB secretly provided a $300,000 loan through the Costa Rican Communist Party to finance his 1970 campaign in exchange for establishing diplomatic ties with the Soviet Union, which he did; he later expanded KGB contacts by providing confidential reports on Central American and Caribbean nations. A 1974 KGB report to Leonid Brezhnev revealed he agreed to publish materials favorable to the KGB, for which he received $10,000 under the guise of stock purchases in his newspaper. In 1981, Figueres acknowledged receiving help from the Central Intelligence Agency, stating he had sought assistance against Latin American dictatorships, was a friend of Allen Dulles, and that the CIA’s Cultural Department helped fund a magazine and youth conferences, though he denied espionage and urged against the Bay of Pigs invasion, which the CIA ignored. He opposed the pre-Castro Cuban regime and sent a planeload of weapons to Cuban insurgents led by Fidel Castro, a member of the Caribbean Legion; after the 1959 Cuban Revolution, a falling out occurred over the growth of Communist influence. In March 1959, during a public speech in Havana, he warned Castro of ideological deviations and was immediately removed from the microphone. He supported John F. Kennedy’s Alliance for Progress but opposed CIA-backed covert operations in Cuba. He was known for his controversial decision to grant asylum to Robert Vesco, a fugitive U.S. financier accused of looting millions from IOS mutual funds, who had personal and business ties to Figueres and contributed to political campaigns in 1974. Figueres stated he would extradite Vesco if requested by the U.S. and attempted to intervene with President Jimmy Carter; the political fallout led to his party losing the 1978 presidential election, after which Vesco fled. In a 1981 interview, Figueres admitted Vesco had "committed many stupidities" but defended asylum, saying he would protect him again if possible, though he regretted that some friends believed he personally benefited. In a 1973 interview, he recalled meeting Vesco in 1972 and that Vesco arranged a $2.15 million investment in Sociedad Agricola Industrial San Cristobal, S.A., a company he co-founded and which employed 3,000 people, making it Costa Rica’s fourth-largest employer. Figueres was well-regarded in Latin America for his center-left ideals and is considered one of the greatest contributors to social democracy. After his presidency, he became a de facto ambassador for future administrations. He supported the left-wing Nicaraguan Revolution that overthrew Anastasio Somoza Debayle in 1979 and criticized U.S. support for the Contras. A proposal for a fourth term in the 1980s was quickly rejected. In a 1986 interview with the Los Angeles Times, he said, "This is an exemplary little country. We are the example for Latin America. In the next century, maybe everyone will be like us." He was a signatory of the agreement to convene a world constitution convention, resulting in the first-ever World Constituent Assembly drafting and adopting the Constitution for the Federation of Earth. He married Henrietta Boggs from the United States in 1941, having two children, Muni and José Martí, before divorcing in 1954; he later married Karen Olsen Beck, also from the United States, with whom he had four children: José María, Karen Christiana, Mariano, and Kirsten. His wife, Karen, was a member of Costa Rica’s Legislative Assembly. He was a close friend of Puerto Rico’s Governor Luis Muñoz Marín, praising his achievements. His son, José María Figueres, served as President from 1994 to 1998. His daughter Muni Figueres Boggs served as Costa Rica’s Ambassador to the United States. His daughter Christiana served as Executive Secretary of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) from 2010 to 2016 and is widely regarded as the architect of the Paris Agreement. He died on 8 June 1990 in San José at age 83 from natural causes and was given a state funeral by the government and former comrades from the 1948 and 1955 revolutions. After the funeral, his remains were taken to La Lucha Sin Fin, his farm since 1928.
